name: P-SSHI
rationale: The reference full-bridge rectifier (FBR) fails because the piezo's open-circuit voltage (3.8V) is lower than the required output (4.5V). I am implementing a Parallel Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor (P-SSHI) circuit. This uses an inductor-switch combination to flip the voltage across the piezo capacitance at its extrema, effectively boosting the voltage seen by the rectifier. I use DSCH Schottky diodes for the full-bridge to minimize losses and a large storage capacitor (4.7uF) to buffer the energy and keep the voltage ripple low and the maximum voltage below 5.5V, especially under strong excitation (S3).

name: P-SSHI-Bleed
rationale: The previous P-SSHI was very close to the target for nominal conditions but suffered from overvoltage in S3 (strong excitation, light load) and high ripple/slow settling. The overvoltage in S3 is caused by the power delivered exceeding the power consumed by the high-impedance load. I am adding a bleeder resistor (R_bleed) in parallel with the load to provide a baseline current sink, which should help clamp the output voltage in S3. To address the ripple and settling issues, the tuner will be encouraged to optimize the balance between the storage capacitor (C1) and the inductor (L1) and the switch time (ton). A larger C1 reduces ripple but slows startup; a smaller L1 reduces the voltage boost and the ripple per pulse. This combination should allow the system to stay within 4.5-5.5 V across all scenarios.

name: Doubler-SSHI
rationale: To specifically address the failure of S4 (weak excitation), where the open-circuit voltage is too low for a standard bridge, I am using a Greinacher voltage doubler. This should boost the output to ~2 * Voc, ensuring S4 reaches the 4.5 V threshold. I combine this with an SSHI inversion stage and a large bleed resistor to keep S3 within the 5.5 V limit.

name: Doubler-SSHI-Boost
rationale: The P-SSHI (Full-Bridge) failed on S4 (too low voltage) and S3 (too high voltage). To fix S4, I replace the full-bridge rectifier with a Greinacher-style voltage-doubler rectifier, which provides an inherent boost to the output voltage. To fix S3 (and S1, S5), I add a bleeder resistor to clamp the output voltage by discarding excess power when the source is strong or the load is light. This combination of a doubler-rectifier and a shunt resistor should shift the output voltage range into the 4.5-5.5V window across all operating conditions.

name: Clamped-Doubler
rationale: The P-SSHI was very close but struggled with the dynamic range between weak excitation (S4) and strong excitation (S3). A full-bridge rectifier's output is limited by Voc, which is too low for S4. A voltage doubler provides a higher gain (approximately 2*Voc), ensuring Vout reaches 4.5V even in S4. To prevent overvoltage in S3, I am implementing a non-linear clamp using a series of Schottky diodes and a Zener diode. A chain of 6 DSCH diodes (~0.25V each) and one DZ33 Zener (3.3V) creates a clamping voltage of approximately 3.3 + 6*0.25 = 4.8V, which keeps the output within the 4.5-5.5V window regardless of the excitation strength or load.

name: S-SECE
rationale: P-SSHI showed strong performance on most conditions but struggled with overvoltage on S3 (where power extraction is too high for the light load) and underpower on S4 (where the boost is insufficient). S-SECE (Symmetric Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction) uses two separate boost paths to transfer the charge of Cp to the output at the voltage extrema. This topology is generally more efficient than P-SSHI and may provide a different power-transfer characteristic that the tuner can better optimize to balance the extreme conditions S3 and S4 while keeping Vout within the 4.5-5.5V window.

name: P-SSHI-Shunt
rationale: The P-SSHI design was highly efficient and almost met all conditions, but lacked voltage regulation, leading to overvoltage on S3 and S5 and under-voltage on S4. I am adding a shunt regulator consisting of a resistor and a 3.3V Zener diode. This creates a leakage path that increases exponentially as Vout rises, clamping the maximum voltage. By optimizing the shunt resistor, we can maintain the output between 4.5V and 5.5V across all operating conditions while leveraging the high power extraction of the SSHI topology.
